learn: Why evaluating open-ended generation is hard
Static, live, arena and model-based benchmarks
intro.why: Every decision in this course (architecture, fine-tuning, prompting, RAG, agents) needs measurement. Choosing the wrong metric gives confident but misleading conclusions.

sections.title: Why evaluation is hard
sections.plain: There are many good answers to most questions, many ways an answer can be good or bad, and test questions leak into training.
sections.body:
Classification has one right label; generation has many acceptable outputs. Quality is multi-dimensional: correctness, faithfulness to sources, helpfulness, harmlessness, style, and also latency and cost. Benchmarks saturate as models improve and leak into web-scale training data.

The evaluation toolbox: intrinsic (perplexity), reference-based (BLEU, ROUGE, METEOR, BERTScore), benchmarks (static, live, arenas, model-graded), factuality/faithfulness checks, LLM-as-a-judge, and human evaluation. Production systems also need task-specific test sets built from real usage and evaluated on every change.

sections.title: Perplexity
sections.plain: How surprised the model is by real text, expressed as the number of equally likely choices it's torn between.
sections.body:
$$\text{PPL} = \exp\Big(-\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N \log p(x_i\mid x_{<i})\Big)$$

Worked: average negative log-likelihood 2.3 → PPL = e^2.3 ≈ 10: on average the model is as uncertain as choosing uniformly among 10 tokens. Token probabilities (0.5, 0.1, 0.25, 0.05) → average NLL 1.844 → PPL 6.32.

Useful for comparing language models on the same held-out text and tokenizer, tracking training and detecting domain shift. Limitations: not comparable across tokenizers, says nothing about helpfulness, truthfulness or instruction following, and aligned chat models often have higher perplexity on raw text despite being more useful.

sections.title: BLEU and ROUGE
sections.plain: Count how many words and word sequences a model's output shares with a human reference.
sections.body:
BLEU (translation): geometric mean of clipped n-gram precisions (n = 1…4) times a brevity penalty BP = exp(1 − r/c) when the candidate is shorter than the reference. ROUGE (summarisation): ROUGE-N = n-gram recall; ROUGE-L uses the longest common subsequence.

Worked: reference "the cat sat quietly on the warm mat" (8 words), candidate "the cat sat on a mat" (6 words), 5 shared words → precision 5/6 = 0.83, recall 5/8 = 0.625, F1 = 0.71. BLEU-2 = 0.717 (brevity penalty) × √(0.83 × 0.40) = 0.41.

Fast, cheap and reproducible, but they reward surface wording: a perfect paraphrase can score low, and a fluent wrong answer with the right words can score high. Use them where references are tight (translation, extraction), not for open-ended chat.

sections.title: METEOR and BERTScore
sections.plain: Give credit for synonyms and similar meanings, not just identical words.
sections.body:
METEOR aligns words using exact matches, stems and synonyms, combines precision and recall with recall weighted higher (F-mean = 10PR/(R + 9P)), and applies a fragmentation penalty for scrambled order. "the feline sat on a rug" gets 5 matches with synonyms versus 3 exact.

BERTScore embeds both texts with a contextual encoder, greedily matches each token to its most similar token in the other text by cosine similarity, and reports precision, recall and F1 of those similarities. In ex1's toy version "feline sat rug" vs "cat sat mat" scores 0.95, where exact-match F1 is 0.33.

Semantic metrics correlate better with human judgement, but still need references and can miss factual errors expressed in plausible vocabulary.

sections.title: Benchmarks
sections.plain: Standard test sets and leaderboards that compare models on the same questions.
sections.body:
• Static benchmarks: fixed question sets for knowledge, reasoning, maths, code (with unit tests), long context, multilinguality. Cheap and reproducible; they saturate and leak.
  • Live / dynamic benchmarks: regularly refreshed questions (e.g. recent contests) to resist contamination.
  • Human arenas: users compare two anonymous models' answers; ratings computed with Elo/Bradley–Terry. Equal ratings, A wins → 1516 vs 1484; a 400-point gap ≈ 91% expected win rate.
  • Model-based benchmarks: an LLM grades open-ended answers against rubrics or references.

Read benchmark results critically: task relevance to your use case, prompt format sensitivity, contamination, variance across runs, and whether gains reflect style rather than capability.

sections.title: Faithfulness and hallucination
sections.plain: Check each claim in an answer against a trusted source or the retrieved documents.
sections.body:
Hallucination: generated content that is unsupported by, or contradicts, the source or world knowledge. Intrinsic hallucinations contradict the given context; extrinsic ones add unverifiable content.

Atomic-fact evaluation (FActScore-style): split an answer into short claims and verify each against a knowledge source. ex2: 4 claims, 3 supported (the Eiffel Tower is not 500 m tall) → factual precision 0.75. For RAG, faithfulness checks claims against the retrieved context (RAGAS-style; 2/3 = 0.67), alongside answer relevance, context precision and context recall.

Verification can use retrieval plus an NLI model or an LLM judge; precision should be paired with completeness so terse answers aren't rewarded unduly.

sections.title: LLM-as-a-judge
sections.plain: Use a strong model to grade answers, while correcting for its predictable biases.
sections.body:
A judge model scores an answer with a rubric (pointwise) or chooses the better of two (pairwise), optionally with a reference answer. It scales to thousands of outputs and correlates reasonably with human preference on many tasks.

Known biases: position (favouring the first or second slot), verbosity (preferring longer answers), self-preference (favouring its own family's style), and weakness on hard reasoning or specialised facts. In ex2, a biased judge picks the first answer 64.8% of the time on equal pairs, and swapping order changes the winner in 55.4% of ties.

Mitigations: evaluate both orders and treat disagreement as a tie, specific rubrics with examples, length control, chain-of-thought before the verdict, multiple judges, and calibration against a human-labelled subset.

sections.title: Human evaluation and benchmark leakage
sections.plain: People are the final judges but are costly and inconsistent; and models may have already seen the test.
sections.body:
Human evaluation captures helpfulness, nuance and harm that automatic metrics miss. Design matters: clear guidelines, trained raters, several raters per item, blind and randomised presentation, pairwise comparisons (easier than absolute scores), and agreement statistics (e.g. Cohen's κ). It is slow and expensive, so it is used for calibration and high-stakes decisions.

Benchmark leakage (contamination): test items appearing in training data inflate scores through memorisation. Detection: n-gram overlap (ex2 finds an 8-gram shared with training text), membership-inference signals, performance drops on rephrased or post-cut-off questions. Prevention: decontaminate training data, keep private held-out sets, use dynamic benchmarks, and report checks.

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• Goodhart again: optimising for a leaderboard can degrade real-world quality.
  • Variance: report confidence intervals and multiple seeds; small differences are often noise.
  • Evaluate the system, not just the model: retrieval, prompts, tools and post-processing all matter.
  • Online metrics (user satisfaction, task completion, escalations) complete offline evaluation.

code.title: Perplexity and reference-based metrics
code.explain: Computes perplexity (e^2.3 ≈ 10; 6.32 for four token probabilities), unigram precision 5/6, recall 5/8 and F1 0.71, BLEU-2 with brevity penalty (0.41), ROUGE-L, a simplified METEOR that credits synonyms, and a BERTScore-style greedy cosine match (0.95 vs exact-match 0.33).
code.notes: Toy embeddings stand in for a contextual encoder.
code.code:
"""Perplexity, unigram precision/recall/F1 (ROUGE-1), BLEU, ROUGE-L, a simplified METEOR, and a BERTScore-style match."""
import math
from collections import Counter
import numpy as np

# Perplexity = exp(average negative log-likelihood per token)
print(f"average NLL 2.3 -> perplexity e^2.3 = {math.exp(2.3):.1f} (as uncertain as choosing among ~10 tokens)")
probs = [0.5, 0.1, 0.25, 0.05]
nll = -sum(math.log(p) for p in probs) / len(probs)
print(f"token probabilities {probs}: avg NLL {nll:.3f}, perplexity {math.exp(nll):.2f}")

ref = "the cat sat quietly on the warm mat".split()       # 8 words
cand = "the cat sat on a mat".split()                      # 6 words
overlap = sum((Counter(cand) & Counter(ref)).values())
P, R = overlap / len(cand), overlap / len(ref)
F = 2 * P * R / (P + R)
print(f"\nreference ({len(ref)} words): {' '.join(ref)}\ncandidate ({len(cand)} words): {' '.join(cand)}")
print(f"unigram overlap {overlap}: precision {overlap}/{len(cand)} = {P:.2f}, recall {overlap}/{len(ref)} = {R:.3f}, F1 = {F:.2f}  (ROUGE-1)")

def ngrams(ws, n): return Counter(tuple(ws[i:i+n]) for i in range(len(ws) - n + 1))
precs = []
for n in (1, 2):
    c, r = ngrams(cand, n), ngrams(ref, n)
    precs.append(sum((c & r).values()) / max(1, sum(c.values())))
bp = 1.0 if len(cand) > len(ref) else math.exp(1 - len(ref) / len(cand))
bleu2 = bp * math.exp(sum(math.log(p) for p in precs) / len(precs))
print(f"BLEU-2: clipped precisions {[round(p, 2) for p in precs]}, brevity penalty {bp:.3f} -> {bleu2:.3f}")

def lcs(a, b):
    T = [[0] * (len(b) + 1) for _ in range(len(a) + 1)]
    for i in range(len(a)):
        for j in range(len(b)):
            T[i+1][j+1] = T[i][j] + 1 if a[i] == b[j] else max(T[i][j+1], T[i+1][j])
    return T[-1][-1]
L = lcs(cand, ref)
print(f"ROUGE-L: longest common subsequence {L} -> recall {L/len(ref):.2f}, precision {L/len(cand):.2f}")

# Simplified METEOR: exact + synonym matches, recall-weighted F-mean, fragmentation penalty
syn = {"rug": "mat", "feline": "cat"}
cand2 = "the feline sat on a rug".split()
m = sum(1 for w in cand2 if w in ref or syn.get(w) in ref)
P2, R2 = m / len(cand2), m / len(ref)
fmean = 10 * P2 * R2 / (R2 + 9 * P2)
print(f"METEOR-style on '{' '.join(cand2)}': {m} matches with synonyms (exact-only would give 3), F-mean {fmean:.2f}")

# BERTScore-style: greedy cosine matching of token embeddings (toy 3-d vectors)
E = {"cat": [1, .1, 0], "feline": [.8, .35, .1], "mat": [0, 1, .1], "rug": [.35, .8, .2], "sat": [0, .1, 1]}
def vec(w): v = np.array(E.get(w, [.3, .3, .3]), float); return v / np.linalg.norm(v)
def bscore(c, r):
    S = np.array([[vec(a) @ vec(b) for b in r] for a in c])
    p, rr = S.max(1).mean(), S.max(0).mean()
    return 2 * p * rr / (p + rr)
print(f"BERTScore-style F1: 'feline sat rug' vs 'cat sat mat' = {bscore(['feline','sat','rug'], ['cat','sat','mat']):.3f} (exact-match F1 would be 0.33)")
code.output:
average NLL 2.3 -> perplexity e^2.3 = 10.0 (as uncertain as choosing among ~10 tokens)
token probabilities [0.5, 0.1, 0.25, 0.05]: avg NLL 1.844, perplexity 6.32

reference (8 words): the cat sat quietly on the warm mat
candidate (6 words): the cat sat on a mat
unigram overlap 5: precision 5/6 = 0.83, recall 5/8 = 0.625, F1 = 0.71  (ROUGE-1)
BLEU-2: clipped precisions [0.83, 0.4], brevity penalty 0.717 -> 0.414
ROUGE-L: longest common subsequence 5 -> recall 0.62, precision 0.83
METEOR-style on 'the feline sat on a rug': 5 matches with synonyms (exact-only would give 3), F-mean 0.64
BERTScore-style F1: 'feline sat rug' vs 'cat sat mat' = 0.952 (exact-match F1 would be 0.33)

code.title: Elo, atomic facts, judge bias and leakage
code.explain: Updates Elo ratings after pairwise wins (1516/1484, then 1531/1469), scores factual precision over atomic claims (0.75) and RAG faithfulness (0.67), simulates a position-biased judge (64.8% first-slot wins; 55.4% flips when swapped), and detects an 8-gram overlap between a test item and training text.
code.notes: Facts are checked against a small hand-labelled set.
code.code:
"""Elo ratings from pairwise votes, atomic-fact precision (FActScore-style), LLM-as-judge position bias, and leakage detection."""
import random

def elo(ra, rb, score_a, k=32):
    ea = 1 / (1 + 10 ** ((rb - ra) / 400))
    return ra + k * (score_a - ea), rb + k * ((1 - score_a) - (1 - ea))
ra, rb = 1500, 1500
print(f"start A {ra}, B {rb}; expected score for A = {1/(1+10**0):.2f}")
ra, rb = elo(ra, rb, 1); print(f"A wins -> A {ra:.0f}, B {rb:.0f}")
ra, rb = elo(ra, rb, 1); print(f"A wins again -> A {ra:.0f}, B {rb:.0f} (smaller gain: the win was more expected)")

# Atomic facts: split an answer into claims and check each against a knowledge source
facts = {"Paris is the capital of France": True, "France has about 68 million people": True,
         "The Eiffel Tower was completed in 1889": True, "The Eiffel Tower is 500 m tall": False}
score = sum(facts.values()) / len(facts)
print(f"\nanswer decomposed into {len(facts)} atomic claims; supported {sum(facts.values())} -> factual precision {score:.2f}")
print("unsupported claim:", [k for k, v in facts.items() if not v][0])
ctx_claims = {"refunds take 14 days": True, "refunds go to the original card": True, "express refunds take 1 day": False}
print(f"faithfulness to retrieved context (RAGAS-style): {sum(ctx_claims.values())}/{len(ctx_claims)} = {sum(ctx_claims.values())/len(ctx_claims):.2f}")

# LLM-as-a-judge position bias: a judge that prefers whichever answer is shown first 65% of the time on ties
random.seed(0)
def judge(first_better):
    if first_better is None: return "first" if random.random() < 0.65 else "second"
    return "first" if first_better else "second"
ties = [judge(None) for _ in range(1000)]
print(f"\non 1000 equally good pairs, judge picks the first answer {ties.count('first')/10:.1f}% of the time")
flips = sum(1 for _ in range(1000) if judge(None) == judge(None))   # same slot both times = different underlying answer
print(f"swapping the order changes which answer wins in {flips/10:.1f}% of ties -> judge both orders and count disagreement as a tie")

# Benchmark leakage: n-gram overlap between a test question and training text
train = "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog near the river bank".split()
test = "a quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog".split()
def grams(ws, n=8): return {tuple(ws[i:i+n]) for i in range(len(ws) - n + 1)}
hit = grams(test) & grams(train)
print(f"\n8-gram overlap between test item and training data: {len(hit)} -> {'possible contamination' if hit else 'clean'}")

start A 1500, B 1500; expected score for A = 0.50
A wins -> A 1516, B 1484
A wins again -> A 1531, B 1469 (smaller gain: the win was more expected)

answer decomposed into 4 atomic claims; supported 3 -> factual precision 0.75
unsupported claim: The Eiffel Tower is 500 m tall
faithfulness to retrieved context (RAGAS-style): 2/3 = 0.67

on 1000 equally good pairs, judge picks the first answer 64.8% of the time
swapping the order changes which answer wins in 55.4% of ties -> judge both orders and count disagreement as a tie

8-gram overlap between test item and training data: 1 -> possible contamination
